#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Container Registry for Backup Scripts
# =============================================================================
# Central source of truth for container IDs and backup configuration.
# Source this file from other backup scripts.
#
# Usage in scripts:
#   source "$(dirname "$0")/containers.sh"
#   VMID=$(get_container_id "openwebui")
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Container ID Mappings
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Format: APP_NAME=CONTAINER_ID
# Add new containers here and they'll be available to all backup scripts

declare -A CONTAINERS=(
    [portainer]=100
    [network-services]=101
    [traefik]=200
    [dashboards]=201
    [authelia]=202
    [immich]=304
    [jellyfin]=401
    [media-management]=402
    [monitoring]=500
    [openwebui]=501
    [n8n]=502
)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Backup Tiers
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Daily: User data that changes frequently (kept 7 days)
# Weekly: Infrastructure that rarely changes (kept 4 weeks)

DAILY_CONTAINERS="304 501 502"      # immich, openwebui, n8n
WEEKLY_CONTAINERS="100 101 200 201 202 401 402 500"  # infrastructure

# All containers to backup (excludes stateless/temporary)
ALL_BACKUP_CONTAINERS="$WEEKLY_CONTAINERS $DAILY_CONTAINERS"

# Excluded from backups (documented here for reference)
# 303 = immich-importer (stateless, runs cron jobs only)
# 600 = desktop-tmp (temporary GUI container)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper Functions
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Get container ID by app name
# Usage: VMID=$(get_container_id "openwebui")
get_container_id() {
    local app="$1"
    echo "${CONTAINERS[$app]:-}"
}

# Get app name by container ID
# Usage: APP=$(get_app_name 501)
get_app_name() {
    local vmid="$1"
    for app in "${!CONTAINERS[@]}"; do
        if [[ "${CONTAINERS[$app]}" == "$vmid" ]]; then
            echo "$app"
            return
        fi
    done
}

# List all app names
# Usage: list_apps
list_apps() {
    echo "${!CONTAINERS[@]}" | tr ' ' '\n' | sort
}

# Check if app exists
# Usage: if app_exists "openwebui"; then ...
app_exists() {
    local app="$1"
    [[ -n "${CONTAINERS[$app]:-}" ]]
}

# Print formatted app list for help messages
print_app_list() {
    echo "Available apps:"
    for app in $(list_apps); do
        printf "  %-20s (ID: %s)\n" "$app" "${CONTAINERS[$app]}"
    done
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Container Registry for Backup Scripts
# =============================================================================
# Central source of truth for container IDs and backup configuration.
# Source this file from other backup scripts.
#
# Usage in scripts:
#   source "$(dirname "$0")/containers.sh"
#   VMID=$(get_container_id "openwebui")
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Container ID Mappings
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Format: APP_NAME=CONTAINER_ID
# Add new containers here and they'll be available to all backup scripts

declare -A CONTAINERS=(
    [portainer]=100
    [network-services]=101
    [traefik]=200
    [dashboards]=201
    [authelia]=202
    [immich]=304
    [jellyfin]=401
    [media-management]=402
    [monitoring]=500
    [openwebui]=501
    [n8n]=502
)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Backup Tiers
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Daily: User data that changes frequently (kept 7 days)
# Weekly: Infrastructure that rarely changes (kept 4 weeks)

DAILY_CONTAINERS="304 501 502"      # immich, openwebui, n8n
WEEKLY_CONTAINERS="100 101 200 201 202 401 402 500"  # infrastructure

# All containers to backup (excludes stateless/temporary)
ALL_BACKUP_CONTAINERS="$WEEKLY_CONTAINERS $DAILY_CONTAINERS"

# Excluded from backups (documented here for reference)
# 303 = immich-importer (stateless, runs cron jobs only)
# 600 = desktop-tmp (temporary GUI container)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper Functions
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Get container ID by app name
# Usage: VMID=$(get_container_id "openwebui")
get_container_id() {
    local app="$1"
    echo "${CONTAINERS[$app]:-}"
}

# Get app name by container ID
# Usage: APP=$(get_app_name 501)
get_app_name() {
    local vmid="$1"
    for app in "${!CONTAINERS[@]}"; do
        if [[ "${CONTAINERS[$app]}" == "$vmid" ]]; then
            echo "$app"
            return
        fi
    done
}

# List all app names
# Usage: list_apps
list_apps() {
    echo "${!CONTAINERS[@]}" | tr ' ' '\n' | sort
}

# Check if app exists
# Usage: if app_exists "openwebui"; then ...
app_exists() {
    local app="$1"
    [[ -n "${CONTAINERS[$app]:-}" ]]
}

# Print formatted app list for help messages
print_app_list() {
    echo "Available apps:"
    for app in $(list_apps); do
        printf "  %-20s (ID: %s)\n" "$app" "${CONTAINERS[$app]}"
    done
}

Based on the search results, here's a comparison of **Duplicati vs Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) vs vzdump** for homelab backup strategies in 2025:

## Proxmox Backup Server (PBS)

**Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) is the go-to choice for Proxmox VE users. It integrates with most storage solutions and supports things like deduplication, encryption, and incremental backups.**(no content)PBS is preferred over built-in snapshots and vzdump facilities because PBS' incremental backups and compression algorithm reduce the amount of space occupied by LXC and VM data, while the deduplication feature ensures you don't accidentally store multiple versions of the same files.(no content)Proxmox Backup Server 4 has native S3 storage targets built into the solution, which is a significant improvement for offsite backups.

You can also install PBS packages directly on the Proxmox node if you want. For a homelab with a single node, this can be acceptable.

## vzdump

vzdump works fine for backing up Proxmox VMs and storing files on a NAS using SMB, but it takes a lot of time because vzdump doesn't work incrementally.(no content)The best solution with respect to completeness and easy-to-use is to virtualize everything and backup everything. PBS can help you with deduplication of backups, but the stock vzdump is not able to do differential backups.(no content)vzdump backups don't need a PBS to be restored but need more space since each snapshot is a full, although compressed, backup archive file.

## Duplicati

Duplicati Version 2 offers chunk deduplication and VSS support, but it is client-only.(no content)Duplicati is useful for backing up Docker container volume data and other file-level backups.

Users have successfully used Duplicati for years to do file-level backups of NAS and desktops to S3 clone services like Wasabi. The mental model includes incremental backups, retention policies with X days/weeks, and client-side encryption.

## Recommended Combined Approach

A popular approach is to use restic or Duplicati for bulk data and the Proxmox VE host operating system, while using PBS for VMs and LXCs so they can be easily restored. Some users also do a vzdump of their PBS VM and back it up with restic on their disk and storage box so they can restore it even if they need to reinstall their Proxmox VE system from scratch.(no content)For VMs and LXCs, PBS is preferred (way more comfortable), but tools like restic or Duplicati work well for raw data.(no content)Using Duplicati to backup the actual data that changes more regularly than the whole VM can complement Proxmox backups, since Proxmox allows restoring the VM to another piece of hardware in case of fire, theft, or disaster.

Based on my search, here's a comparison of Duplicati backup versus Proxmox's native vzdump for LXC containers:

## Proxmox vzdump (Native Backup Tool)

Proxmox VE backups are always full backups - containing the VM/CT configuration and all data. Backups can be started via the GUI or via the vzdump command-line tool.(no content)The vzdump tool, as one of the core components of Proxmox VE, provides powerful support for the backup and restoration of virtual machines and containers. vzdump is a command-line utility in Proxmox VE for creating backups of VMs and containers.

**Storage Options:**
Backup storage can either be a Proxmox Backup Server storage, where backups are stored as de-duplicated chunks and metadata, or a file-level storage, where backups are stored as regular files. Using Proxmox Backup Server on a dedicated host is recommended, because of its advanced features.

**LXC Backup Performance Limitations (2025):**
The core issue relates to backup speeds for LXC containers using Proxmox and PBS. Small LXC Containers (50GB or less) perform relatively well, but larger containers (500GB) can have very slow backups (around 12 hours). This is because KVM backups have "CBT change block tracking" style backups for more efficient deltas, while LXC backups don't have this feature - requiring a multi-step rsync process, then comparing the latest backup data against existing backups to send over deltas.

**Deduplication:**
Proxmox Backup Server is highly recommended for backing up VMs. It's a separate but related product for backing up Proxmox VE VMs and handles deduplication and retention policies.

## Duplicati in Proxmox LXC

If you wish to share the files or access the files directly from cloud storage for other purposes, you may not want to use Duplicati. The purpose of Duplicati is for backing up and restoring data securely. Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive comparison of Restic, BorgBackup, and Duplicati for homelab backups in 2025:

## Overview

In 2025, three names keep popping up for backup solutions: Duplicacy, Restic, and Borg. Each has its fanbase, quirks, and magic.(no content)All three are open-source, deduplicating, and support encrypted backups.

## Key Differences

### Deduplication
- Duplicacy uses global deduplication—all clients backing up to the same storage share chunks, so you save space if you have similar data across servers. This is a killer feature for fleets of VPSes or Docker hosts.
- Restic & Borg deduplicate within each repository. If you back up two servers to the same repo, they'll deduplicate, but if you use separate repos, no cross-deduplication.

### Cloud Storage Support
- Duplicacy is a Swiss army knife—supports S3, Backblaze B2, Google Drive, Azure, Dropbox, SFTP, WebDAV, local, and more.
- Restic supports S3, B2, Azure, SFTP, REST server, local, and more.
- Borg supports Local, SSH, SFTP. For cloud, you'll need rclone or similar.
- Restic offers native S3 support with excellent compatibility across providers. It supports server-side encryption, custom endpoints, and works seamlessly with Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, and traditional Amazon S3. The implementation is mature and handles network interruptions gracefully with automatic retry mechanisms.

### Encryption
- All three encrypt data before it leaves your server. No plaintext in the cloud. Restic and Duplicacy use AES-GCM; Borg uses authenticated encryption (AES-CTR + HMAC).
- Restic uses AES-256 encryption in counter mode with Poly1305 authentication. Keys are derived using scrypt, providing strong protection against brute-force attacks. All metadata, including file names and directory structures, is encrypted.
- BorgBackup implements AES-256 encryption with HMAC-SHA256 authentication. It offers multiple encryption modes, including authenticated encryption and key-based encryption. Borg's approach to key management is particularly robust, with options for both passphrase and key file authentication.

### Performance
- While Restic used slightly more CPU and RAM, it stood out with faster backup creation times. The average was approximately 111.517 seconds, compared to Borg's 211.332 seconds.
- For instances with limited RAM (2GB or less), BorgBackup's memory efficiency makes it the clear choice.

### Reliability Concerns

**Restic:**
- Restic in particular just works and is ridiculously easy to set up and use without any complicated commands. And it's exceptionally reliable: I have had to do restores many times with this tool from small and large repositories and it has never failed me, never.
- Unlike Borg, Restic repositories showed no cases of corruption in their analysis.

**Duplicati:**
- Frequent crashes furthered distrust of the program in case it's ever needed to restore data. There are some horror stories circulating around various forums about Duplicati corrupting data or just displaying poor restore performance.
- One user noted that Duplicati was resources intensive & very slow.
- Duplicati was very unreliable with large backups for some users. One commenter noted they never managed to do a full restore with Duplicati.

**Borg:**
- Borg has always looked rock solid as well.
- BorgBackup excels in performance-critical scenarios where local storage is preferred.

### User Interface
- Borg is very easy to run periodically using a cronjob and seems very stable and widely used. However, for backing up family members' personal devices, there needs to be a GUI available. For Borg a GUI named Vorta can be installed separately but Vorta is not available for Windows.
- Restic is not very convenient to set up on Windows. Restic provides the basis for making backups, deduplication, and encryption but you have to script the backup schedule yourself.

## Recommendations

- Restic provides the best balance of features and ecosystem compatibility, making it ideal for mixed environments and S3-based workflows.
- Borg's cloud support is clunky (needs rclone or SSHFS). Use Borg for local or SSH backups; for cloud, consider Restic or Duplicacy.
- The main reason some choose Restic over Borg is the support for backends other than sftp. The cheapest storage these days is object storage such as Backblaze B2 and Wasabi. With Restic you have the option to quickly add a new cloud backup target.

### Also Worth Considering: Kopia
Kopia is a new kid on the block—cross-platform, deduplicating, fast, with a slick GUI.(no content)Kopia was designed with cloud storage in mind, offering the most comprehensive S3 support. It includes advanced features like parallel uploads, configurable chunk sizes for optimal cloud performance, and built-in support for storage classes and lifecycle policies.

However, some users report that Kopia is promising, but it's not reliable enough yet. On one server during testing, it corrupted the repository 3 times in a row, until the user gave up and switched back to Restic.

content.text:
Here's my analysis comparing your current setup vs Duplicati and other alternatives:

## Your Current Setup

| Pros | Cons |
|------|------|
| Native Proxmox integration (vzdump) | Manual script maintenance |
| Full VM/CT restore capability | No deduplication (full backups) |
| Pre-backup hooks for databases | More storage used |
| rclone crypt for B2 encryption | Scripts spread across multiple files |
| Two-tier retention (daily/weekly) | |

## Duplicati Assessment

**I would not recommend Duplicati** for your use case. Here's why:

1. **Reliability issues** - Duplicati has well-documented problems with [backup corruption](https://forum.duplicati.com/t/why-the-negative-reviews/19693), especially on Linux. Users report [database corruption](https://forum.duplicati.com/t/using-dupicati-for-years-backup-suddenly-broke-getting-worse/20500) when backups are interrupted, and some have [never successfully completed a full restore](https://forum.duplicati.com/t/big-comparison-borg-vs-restic-vs-arq-5-vs-duplicacy-vs-duplicati/9952).

2. **Wrong abstraction layer** - Duplicati does file-level backups. Your vzdump backups capture the entire LXC container state including Proxmox config, which means you can restore a container to any Proxmox host. Duplicati would only back up files, not the container itself.

3. **You'd still need vzdump** - For disaster recovery (restore LXC to new hardware), you need vzdump. Adding Duplicati would be *extra* complexity, not a replacement.

## Better Alternatives to Consider

### Option 1: Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) - **Best fit for your setup**

[PBS is purpose-built for Proxmox](https://www.virtualizationhowto.com/2025/10/ultimate-home-lab-backup-strategy-2025-edition/) and offers:
- **Incremental backups** - vzdump is always full; PBS deduplicates
- **Native integration** - shows up in Proxmox UI, easy restores
- **Deduplication** - significant storage savings
- **Can run on Proxmox host** - no separate hardware needed for homelab
- **PBS 4 has native S3 targets** - direct cloud backup without rclone scripts

This would eliminate your vzdump storage bloat while keeping native restore capability.

### Option 2: Restic for cloud sync (replace rclone)

If you want to keep vzdump but improve cloud backups, [restic is more reliable than Duplicati](https://mangohost.net/blog/duplicacy-vs-restic-vs-borg-which-backup-tool-is-right-in-2025/):
- Native B2 support
- Deduplication at the cloud layer
- Rock-solid reliability ("never failed" in user reports)
- Encryption built-in

You'd run: `restic -r b2:bucket backup /tank/backups/vzdump`

### Option 3: Keep current setup (it's actually fine)

Your current setup is not as "manual" as you might think:
- `containers.sh` centralizes definitions
- `jobs.cfg` handles scheduling
- `pre-backup-hook.sh` handles database dumps
- Cloud sync runs automatically via cron

The only maintenance is adding new containers to `containers.sh`.

## Recommendation

**For your homelab, I'd suggest PBS** if you want to reduce complexity:

| Current | With PBS |
|---------|----------|
| vzdump full backups | Incremental deduped backups |
| Manual rclone scripts | Native S3 sync (PBS 4) |
| Hook scripts for DBs | Same (still needed) |
| ~30GB per backup | ~5-10GB incremental |

PBS can run as an LXC or directly on your Proxmox host. It integrates directly into the Proxmox UI for scheduling and restore.

Would you like me to research setting up PBS on your existing Proxmox host?

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Proxmox Backup Server's deduplication efficiency for large files like photos and media:

## Key Findings

### How PBS Deduplication Works

Backups are sent incrementally from the client to the Proxmox Backup Server, where data is then deduplicated.(no content)Periodic backups usually produce large amounts of duplicate data. The deduplication layer in the Proxmox Backup solution reduces the amount of duplicate data, reducing the physical space required for data storage.

### Chunking Strategy for Files

When working with file-based systems rather than block-based systems, using fixed-sized chunks is not a good idea, since every time a file would change in size, the remaining data would be shifted around, resulting in many chunks changing and the amount of deduplication being reduced. To improve this, Proxmox Backup Server uses dynamically sized chunks instead.(no content)For fidx/VM/block device backups, chunk size is static 4MB, for didx/CT/file level/pxar backups, it's dynamically calculated within certain limits.

### Deduplication Efficiency for Photos/Media

An identical file A in two containers can end up being represented as one or more chunks and be deduplicated, or end up in a chunk with file B in one container, and file C in another, and not be deduplicated. So deduplication will work more reliably with snapshots of one source (chances for the chunker to split the input stream into chunks at similar boundaries are higher).

### Real-World Deduplication Ratios

Users have reported varying deduplication factors:
- Some users see deduplication factors of 62, where backups use 195 GB of storage space but would need 12 TB to restore all of them.
- Other users report deduplication factors as high as 324, where backups use around 323GB on the datastore but the original data usage is 94.86 TiB.

### Important Considerations

The deduplication domain is a datastore. Note that encryption creates another layer on top, so the same data encrypted with different keys will not be deduplicated even if stored in the same datastore (since the stored encrypted data is different).(no content)There is a "Deduplication Factor" on the summary page for each datastore that gives you a hint as to how much space is saved by dedup. Note: You have to run a garbage collection on the store for this to update.

### Compression

The ultra-fast Zstandard compression is able to compress several gigabytes of data per second.

**Summary**: PBS can be efficient for backing up photos and media, especially when backing up the same source repeatedly. However, deduplication across different sources (different VMs/containers) may be less effective due to how chunk boundaries are calculated. Photos and media files that are already compressed (JPEG, MP4, etc.) won't benefit much from PBS's compression but can still benefit from deduplication across multiple backup snapshots.

content.text:
**Short answer: PBS is not ideal for raw photo backups.**

Here's why:

## PBS Photo Backup Limitations

1. **Compressed files don't dedupe well** - Your photos (JPEG, HEIC) and videos (MP4) are already compressed. PBS's [deduplication works on chunks](https://pbs.proxmox.com/docs/technical-overview.html), but compressed media files have poor chunk alignment - small metadata changes can shift all subsequent chunks.

2. **Designed for VM/CT backups** - PBS excels at backing up system state where most data stays the same between snapshots. Photos are mostly "write once, read many" - each photo is unique, so there's nothing to deduplicate.

3. **Your photos live outside LXCs** - Your photos are on `/tank/photos` (ZFS), mounted into the immich-importer container. PBS backs up containers, not arbitrary directories.

## Your Current Photo Backup (Already Good)

Your setup with rclone crypt → B2 is actually the right approach for photos:

```
LXC 303 (/photos) → rclone crypt → Backblaze B2
```

- **rclone handles large files efficiently** - streams directly, no chunking overhead
- **B2 is cheap for cold storage** - $6/TB/month
- **Encryption at rest** - rclone crypt before upload

## Recommended Hybrid Approach

| Data Type | Backup Method | Why |
|-----------|---------------|-----|
| LXC containers | PBS | Incremental, deduped, native restore |
| Photos/media | rclone → B2 | Direct sync, cheaper, better for large files |
| Database dumps | PBS (with containers) or rclone | Small, compressible |

## If You Want "One Solution"

**Restic** could unify both:
- Backs up both files and directories
- Native B2 support with deduplication
- Works well with photos (content-defined chunking)
- Single tool for everything

But honestly, your current split approach (vzdump for containers, rclone for photos) matches the data characteristics well. PBS would improve the container backup side but wouldn't replace your photo backup.

**Bottom line**: Add PBS for better LXC backups, keep rclone for photos.

Sources:
- [PBS Technical Overview](https://pbs.proxmox.com/docs/technical-overview.html)
- [PBS deduplication for photos discussion](https://forum.proxmox.com/threads/proxmox-backup-client-to-backup-photos-strange-deduplication-factor-and-long-backup-backup-time-after-some-days.85703/)
- [PBS Features](https://www.proxmox.com/en/products/proxmox-backup-server/features)

Perfect! Now I have a comprehensive understanding. Let me create a summary report.

## OpenTofu Homelab Setup - Comprehensive Summary

Based on my exploration of the repository, here's a complete analysis of the OpenTofu infrastructure setup:

### 1. STANDARD PATTERN FOR ADDING A NEW APP

The pattern follows this structure:

```
tofu/apps/<app-name>/
├── main.tf                    # Core app configuration (required)
├── terraform.tfstate          # Encrypted state file
├── ip-registry.tf -> ../../   # Symlink to central IP registry
├── shared.tf -> ../../        # Symlink to shared variables
├── versions.tf -> ../../      # Symlink to provider versions
├── onepassword.tf -> ../../   # Symlink to 1Password secrets
└── deploy/                    # Docker Compose and config files
    ├── docker-compose.yml     # Primary deployment file
    └── [service-dirs]/        # Service-specific configs
```

### 2. KEY FILES NEEDED

**Required files in app directory:**
- `main.tf` - Contains the docker-lxc module instantiation and traefik-route modules
- Symlinks to shared files: `shared.tf`, `versions.tf`, `onepassword.tf`, `ip-registry.tf`
- `.terraform.lock.hcl` - Generated during tofu init

**Required files in deploy/ directory:**
- `docker-compose.yml` - Defines all services for the app
- Service configuration directories (e.g., `openwebui/`, `ollama/` for openwebui app)

**Optional per-app files:**
- `.env` - Environment variables (not tracked, or listed in deploy root)
- `.env.template` - Template for required env vars
- Generation scripts (e.g., `generate-env.sh`)

### 3. DOCKER-LXC MODULE ARCHITECTURE

**Module Location:** `/Users/rambhiad/Code/Repositories/personal-projects/homelab/tofu/modules/docker-lxc/`

**Core Functionality:**
1. **Wraps lxc-base module** - Creates privileged LXC container with static IP
2. **File Synchronization** - Uses `filesync` provider to sync deploy dir to `/config` in container
3. **SSH Access** - Configures root SSH access with ed25519 key
4. **Proxmox Integration** - Auto-generates detailed notes in Proxmox UI with:
   - Service description and URLs
   - Exposed ports and services
   - Quick command reference
   - SSH connection info
5. **Mount Points** - Supports additional storage mounts (e.g., `/photos`, `/data`, `/cache`)
6. **Docker-Ready** - Uses Docker-preinstalled template (Debian 13)

**Key Module Variables:**
- `name` - Container name
- `container_id` - Proxmox VM ID (100-254 range)
- `ip_address` - Static IP in CIDR format (e.g., "192.168.1.221/24")
- `deploy_dir` - Local path to deployment files
- `cores`, `memory`, `swap` - Resource allocation
- `rootfs_storage` - Storage pool (nvme-containers or tank)
- `mount_points` - Additional volumes from host
- `unprivileged` - false for Docker/GPU access
- `service_urls`, `services`, `custom_notes` - Proxmox documentation

### 4. OPENWEBUI IP ALLOCATION

**Current Configuration:**
- **Container ID:** 501
- **IP Address:** 192.168.1.221 (confirmed in ip-registry.tf and main.tf)
- **Domain (Internal):** ai.homelab.rambtech.dev
- **Direct Access:** http://192.168.1.221:3000

**From ip-registry.tf (line 57):**
```hcl
openwebui = "192.168.1.221"  # LXC 501 - AI chat
```

**From container_ips mapping (line 143):**
```hcl
501 = local.ip_registry.apps.openwebui
```

### 5. SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR SETUP

**Network & Security:**
- All static IPs tracked in `tofu/ip-registry.tf` (symlinked to each app)
- IP ranges organized: 1-99 (infrastructure), 100-149 (core), 150-199 (LXC preferred), 200-224 (reserved)
- Traefik (LXC 200, IP: 192.168.1.235) handles all HTTPS/routing
- Two domain structures: `*.homelab.rambtech.dev` (internal) and `*.rambtech.dev` (public via Cloudflare)

**State Management:**
- All state files encrypted with PBKDF2 + AES-GCM
- Safe to commit to git
- Passphrase provided via `TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase` (from 1Password)

**Provider Configuration:**
- Proxmox API: via 1Password (`op://homelab/opentofu/password`)
- Cloudflare API: via 1Password (sections: tunnel_token, ddns_api_token)
- SSH: ed25519 keys at `~/.ssh/homelab_ed25519`
- 1Password CLI v2.23.0+ required with biometric auth

**Secrets Integration:**
- Centralized in `tofu/onepassword.tf` (symlinked to all apps)
- 1Password vault: "homelab"
- Key secrets: proxmox_api_token, cloudflare_api_token, grafana_admin_password, discord_webhook_url
- Custom field access via flattening sections

**Traefik Route Self-Registration:**
- Each app module includes `traefik-route` modules for self-service registration
- Routes automatically synced to Traefik LXC (`192.168.1.235`)
- Supports both internal (websecure/Let's Encrypt) and public (web/Cloudflare tunnel) routes
- Example from openwebui:
  ```hcl
  module "openwebui_route" {
    source = "../../modules/traefik-route"
    app_name    = "openwebui"
    backend_url = "http://${module.openwebui.ip_address}:3000"
    internal_domain = "ai.${var.domain_internal}"
  }
  ```

**Deployment Structure:**
- Docker Compose files synced to `/config` on each container
- Manual `docker compose up -d` required (or can be automated via post_sync_commands)
- Each service gets its own subdirectory in deploy (e.g., deploy/openwebui/, deploy/ollama/)
- Services can share networks via docker-compose

**Resource Allocation Examples:**
- Dashboards (201): 2 cores, 4GB RAM
- Monitoring (500): 4 cores, 4GB RAM  
- Immich (304): 18 cores, 6GB RAM (GPU intensive)
- OpenWebUI (501): 12 cores, 24GB RAM (LLM acceleration)
- Media Management (402): 4 cores, 8GB RAM

**GPU Acceleration:**
- Supported via device passthrough (AMD Radeon 890M used)
- Applied to immich (ML features) and openwebui (Ollama ROCM)
- Devices passed: `/dev/dri/card0`, `/dev/dri/renderD128`, `/dev/kfd`

**Backup Integration:**
- Pre-backup hooks available (used by immich for DB dumps)
- Monitoring stack (500) includes Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Uptime Kuma, ntfy
- ntfy used for Discord alerting

### 6. EXAMPLE APP CONFIGURATIONS

**Minimal App (Dashboards):**
```hcl
module "dashboards" {
  source = "../../modules/docker-lxc"
  name         = "dashboards"
  container_id = 201
  ip_address   = "${local.ip_registry.apps.dashboards}/24"
  deploy_dir   = "${path.module}/deploy"
  # ... rest of config
}
```

**App with Mount Points (Immich):**
```hcl
mount_points = [
  { slot = 0, path = "/photos", volume = "/tank/photos" },
  { slot = 1, path = "/cache", volume = "/tank/cache/immich" }
]
```

**App with Multiple Routes (Monitoring):**
- 5 separate traefik-route modules (grafana, prometheus, alertmanager, uptime_kuma, ntfy)
- Each auto-syncs YAML config to Traefik container

**Complete File Structure View:**

```
dashboards/                    monitoring/                 openwebui/
├── main.tf                    ├── main.tf                 ├── main.tf
├── shared.tf -> ../../        ├── shared.tf -> ../../     ├── shared.tf -> ../../
├── versions.tf -> ../../      ├── versions.tf -> ../../   ├── versions.tf -> ../../
├── ip-registry.tf -> ../../   ├── ip-registry.tf -> ../../├── ip-registry.tf -> ../../
├── onepassword.tf -> ../../   ├── onepassword.tf -> ../../├── onepassword.tf -> ../../
└── deploy/                    └── deploy/                 └── deploy/
    ├── docker-compose.yml         ├── docker-compose.yml      ├── docker-compose.yml
    ├── homepage/                  ├── prometheus/             ├── openwebui/
    └── dashy/                     ├── grafana/                └── ollama/
                                   └── alertmanager/
```

All files are at: `/Users/rambhiad/Code/Repositories/personal-projects/homelab/tofu/`

# =============================================================================
# OpenWebUI LXC - AI Chat Interface with Ollama
# =============================================================================
# Container ID: 501
# IP: 192.168.1.221
#
# Uses the docker-lxc module - the gold standard pattern for Docker apps.
# Features AMD GPU passthrough for Ollama LLM acceleration.
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Variables
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

variable "container_id" {
  type    = number
  default = 501
}

variable "cores" {
  type    = number
  default = 12
}

variable "memory" {
  type    = number
  default = 24576
}

variable "rootfs_size" {
  type    = number
  default = 64
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# OpenWebUI Container
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

module "openwebui" {
  source = "../../modules/docker-lxc"

  name         = "openwebui"
  container_id = var.container_id
  proxmox_node = var.proxmox_node

  # Network
  ip_address = "${local.ip_registry.apps.openwebui}/24"
  gateway    = "192.168.1.1"

  # Resources
  cores  = var.cores
  memory = var.memory
  swap   = 2048

  rootfs_storage = "nvme-containers"
  rootfs_size    = var.rootfs_size

  # Privileged for Docker
  unprivileged = false

  # Deployment
  deploy_dir  = "${path.module}/deploy"
  target_path = "/config"

  # SSH
  ssh_public_key       = local.ssh_public_key
  ssh_private_key_path = var.ssh_private_key_path
  proxmox_ssh_host     = var.proxmox_ssh_host

  # Template with Docker pre-installed
  template = var.lxc_template_docker

  # Proxmox Notes
  service_name        = "OpenWebUI"
  service_description = "AI chat interface with Ollama backend (AMD GPU accelerated)"

  service_urls = {
    internal = "https://ai.${var.domain_internal}"
    direct   = "http://192.168.1.221:3000"
  }

  services = [
    { name = "OpenWebUI", port = 3000, info = "AI chat interface" },
    { name = "Ollama", port = 11434, info = "LLM backend (ROCM GPU)" },
    { name = "Portainer Agent", port = 9001, info = "Container management agent" }
  ]

  custom_notes = <<-EOT
## GPU Acceleration

AMD Radeon 890M passed through for Ollama LLM acceleration:
- `/dev/kfd`, `/dev/dri` devices
- ROCM backend

**Check GPU:**
```
docker exec ollama rocminfo
```

## Quick Commands

**View logs:**
```
cd /config && docker compose logs -f openwebui
cd /config && docker compose logs -f ollama
```

**List models:**
```
docker exec ollama ollama list
```

**Pull new model:**
```
docker exec ollama ollama pull llama3.2
```

## Managed by OpenTofu

Run `task tofu:apply APP=openwebui` to update.
EOT

  tags = ["openwebui", "ai", "ollama", "llm"]
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Traefik Route - Self-Service Route Registration
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

module "openwebui_route" {
  source = "../../modules/traefik-route"

  app_name    = "openwebui"
  backend_url = "http://${module.openwebui.ip_address}:3000"

  # Internal route (HTTPS via Let's Encrypt)
  internal_domain = "ai.${var.domain_internal}"

  # Traefik config
  traefik_host         = local.ip_registry.core.traefik
  ssh_private_key_path = var.ssh_private_key_path

  # Middlewares
  internal_middlewares = ["security-headers"]

  depends_on = [module.openwebui]
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Outputs
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

output "container_id" {
  value = module.openwebui.container_id
}

output "ip_address" {
  value = module.openwebui.ip_address
}

output "ssh_command" {
  value = module.openwebui.ssh_command
}

output "urls" {
  value = {
    internal = module.openwebui_route.internal_url
    direct   = "http://${module.openwebui.ip_address}:3000"
  }
}

output "traefik_config_path" {
  description = "Path to Traefik config on Traefik LXC"
  value       = module.openwebui_route.remote_config_path
}

# =============================================================================
# Docker LXC Module
# =============================================================================
# Opinionated module for deploying Docker-based applications in LXC containers.
# Uses lxc-base + filesync provider + remotedockercompose provider for a
# fully declarative deployment experience.
# =============================================================================

terraform {
  required_providers {
    proxmox = {
      source  = "bpg/proxmox"
      version = "~> 0.69"
    }
    filesync = {
      source  = "darshan-rambhia/filesync"
      version = "~> 0.3"
    }
  }
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# LXC Container
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

module "lxc" {
  source = "../lxc-base"

  name         = var.name
  container_id = var.container_id
  proxmox_node = var.proxmox_node

  # Network
  ip_address     = var.ip_address
  gateway        = var.gateway
  network_bridge = "vmbr0"

  # Resources
  cores  = var.cores
  memory = var.memory
  swap   = var.swap

  rootfs_storage = var.rootfs_storage
  rootfs_size    = var.rootfs_size

  # Container type
  unprivileged = var.unprivileged
  template     = var.template

  # SSH
  ssh_public_key               = var.ssh_public_key
  proxmox_ssh_host             = var.proxmox_ssh_host
  proxmox_ssh_private_key_path = var.ssh_private_key_path

  # Features
  enable_nesting = true
  enable_keyctl  = true
  enable_fuse    = false

  # Mount points
  mount_points = var.mount_points

  # Proxmox notes
  description = var.enable_proxmox_notes ? templatefile("${path.module}/templates/notes.md.tftpl", {
    service_name = var.service_name != "" ? var.service_name : var.name
    description  = var.service_description
    urls         = var.service_urls
    services     = var.services
    ssh_host     = split("/", var.ip_address)[0]
    custom_notes = var.custom_notes
    managed_by   = true
  }) : ""

  # Tags
  tags = concat(["docker"], var.tags)
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# File Sync - Using filesync provider directly
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Get list of all files in deploy directory, excluding specified patterns
locals {
  _all_deploy_files = var.deploy_dir != "" ? fileset(var.deploy_dir, "**") : []

  # Filter out files matching exclude patterns
  deploy_files = [
    for f in local._all_deploy_files : f
    if !anytrue([for pattern in var.exclude_patterns : can(regex(pattern, f))])
  ]
}

# Sync each file individually using filesync provider
resource "filesync_file" "config_files" {
  for_each = toset(local.deploy_files)

  source      = "${var.deploy_dir}/${each.value}"
  destination = "${var.target_path}/${each.value}"
  host        = module.lxc.ip_address
  mode        = "0644"

  # SSH configuration - provider config is inherited but explicit for clarity
  ssh_user     = "root"
  ssh_key_path = var.ssh_private_key_path

  depends_on = [module.lxc]
}

# Set custom permissions for specific files
resource "filesync_file" "custom_permissions" {
  for_each = var.file_permissions

  source      = "${var.deploy_dir}/${trimsuffix(trimprefix(each.key, var.target_path), "/")}"
  destination = each.key
  host        = module.lxc.ip_address
  mode        = each.value

  # SSH configuration
  ssh_user     = "root"
  ssh_key_path = var.ssh_private_key_path

  depends_on = [filesync_file.config_files]
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Docker Compose
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Note: Docker Compose stack deployment is handled by the deploy directory
# containing docker-compose.yml. The filesync provider syncs the compose file
# to the container. Applications can manually run `docker compose up -d` via
# SSH if needed, or include it in post_sync_commands.

# Homelab Infrastructure Automation
# https://taskfile.dev

version: '3'

vars:
  PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.TASKFILE_DIR}}"
  TOFU_DIR: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}/tofu"

env:
  # State encryption passphrase - MUST be TF_VAR because encryption runs before providers
  # All other secrets are now fetched via 1Password provider directly in OpenTofu
  TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase:
    sh: |
      if [ -n "$TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase" ]; then
        echo "$TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase"
      else
        op read "op://homelab/opentofu/password" 2>/dev/null || echo ""
      fi

# =============================================================================
# Included Taskfiles (flattened into main namespace)
# =============================================================================
includes:
  tofu:
    taskfile: ./tasks/tofu.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"
  backup:
    taskfile: ./tasks/backup.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"
  cloud:
    taskfile: ./tasks/cloud.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"
  template:
    taskfile: ./tasks/template.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"

tasks:
  # ===========================================================================
  # Desktop LXC (Temporary GUI for Downloads)
  # ===========================================================================

  desktop:create:
    desc: "Create temporary GUI desktop LXC for downloading Google Takeout"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/desktop-lxc/create.sh

  desktop:destroy:
    desc: "Destroy temporary GUI desktop LXC"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/desktop-lxc/destroy.sh

  desktop:info:
    desc: "Show VNC connection info for desktop LXC"
    cmds:
      - |
        IP=$(ssh root@homelab "pct exec 600 -- ip -4 addr show eth0 | grep inet | awk '{print \$2}' | cut -d/ -f1" 2>/dev/null)
        if [ -z "$IP" ]; then
          echo "Desktop LXC (600) is not running or does not exist."
          echo "Run 'task desktop:create' first."
          exit 1
        fi
        echo "=== Desktop LXC VNC Connection ==="
        echo ""
        echo "VNC Host: $IP:5901"
        echo ""
        echo "macOS: Open Finder, Cmd+K, enter vnc://$IP:5901"
        echo ""
        echo "Downloads save to: /downloads (mounted to /tank/photo-import)"

  desktop:restart-vnc:
    desc: "Restart VNC server on desktop LXC"
    cmds:
      - |
        echo "Restarting VNC server..."
        ssh root@homelab "pct exec 600 -- bash -c 'vncserver -kill :1 2>/dev/null || true; vncserver :1 -geometry 1920x1080 -depth 24 -localhost no'"
        echo "VNC server restarted on display :1"

  # ===========================================================================
  # Authelia Operations
  # ===========================================================================

  authelia:secrets:
    desc: "Generate Authelia secrets from 1Password"
    cmds:
      - |
        SECRETS_DIR="{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}/tofu/apps/authelia/deploy/secrets"
        mkdir -p "$SECRETS_DIR"
        echo "Fetching secrets from 1Password..."
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/jwt_secret" > "$SECRETS_DIR/jwt_secret"
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/session_secret" > "$SECRETS_DIR/session_secret"
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/storage_encryption_key" > "$SECRETS_DIR/storage_encryption_key"

1→# OpenTofu IaC Commands
     2→# https://taskfile.dev
     3→#
     4→# Each app has its own state file in tofu/apps/<app>/
     5→# Use APP=dashboards|openwebui|portainer|etc to specify which app
     6→
     7→version: '3'
     8→
     9→vars:
    10→  TOFU_DIR: "tofu"
    11→
    12→tasks:
    13→  tofu:init:
    14→    desc: "Initialize OpenTofu for an app (APP=dashboards|openwebui|portainer)"
    15→    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    16→    cmds:
    17→      - tofu init
    18→    requires:
    19→      vars: [APP]
    20→
    21→  tofu:plan:
    22→    desc: "Plan infrastructure changes for an app"
    23→    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    24→    cmds:
    25→      - pwd
    26→      - tofu plan -out=tfplan
    27→    requires:
    28→      vars: [APP]
    29→    preconditions:
    30→      - sh: test -d .terraform
    31→        msg: "Run 'task tofu:init APP={{.APP}}' first"
    32→
    33→  tofu:apply:
    34→    desc: "Apply planned infrastructure changes for an app"
    35→    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    36→    cmds:
    37→      - tofu apply tfplan
    38→    requires:
    39→      vars: [APP]
    40→    preconditions:
    41→      - sh: test -f tfplan
    42→        msg: "Run 'task tofu:plan APP={{.APP}}' first"
    43→
    44→  tofu:apply:auto:
    45→    desc: "Plan and apply without confirmation"
    46→    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    47→    cmds:
    48→      - tofu apply -auto-approve
    49→    requires:
    50→      vars: [APP]
    51→
    52→  tofu:destroy:
    53→    desc: "Destroy an app's infrastructure"
    54→    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    55→    cmds:
    56→      - echo "⚠️  This will destroy {{.APP}} infrastructure!"
    57→      - tofu destroy

# OpenTofu IaC Commands
# https://taskfile.dev
#
# Each app has its own state file in tofu/apps/<app>/
# Use APP=dashboards|openwebui|portainer|etc to specify which app

version: '3'

vars:
  TOFU_DIR: "tofu"

tasks:
  tofu:init:
    desc: "Initialize OpenTofu for an app (APP=dashboards|openwebui|portainer)"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu init
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:plan:
    desc: "Plan infrastructure changes for an app"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - pwd
      - tofu plan -out=tfplan
    requires:
      vars: [APP]
    preconditions:
      - sh: test -d .terraform
        msg: "Run 'task tofu:init APP={{.APP}}' first"

  tofu:apply:
    desc: "Apply planned infrastructure changes for an app"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu apply tfplan
    requires:
      vars: [APP]
    preconditions:
      - sh: test -f tfplan
        msg: "Run 'task tofu:plan APP={{.APP}}' first"

  tofu:apply:auto:
    desc: "Plan and apply without confirmation"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu apply -auto-approve
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:destroy:
    desc: "Destroy an app's infrastructure"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - echo "⚠️  This will destroy {{.APP}} infrastructure!"
      - tofu destroy
    requires:
      vars: [APP]
    prompt: "Are you sure you want to destroy {{.APP}}?"

  tofu:output:
    desc: "Show infrastructure outputs for an app"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu output
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:state:
    desc: "List all resources in an app's state"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu state list
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:fmt:
    desc: "Format all Terraform files"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu fmt -recursive

  tofu:validate:
    desc: "Validate an app's configuration"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu validate
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:encryption:setup:
    desc: "Set up state encryption passphrase in 1Password"
    cmds:
      - |
        echo "Creating 1Password item for state encryption..."
        PASSPHRASE=$(openssl rand -base64 32)
        op item create \
          --category=password \
          --title="opentofu" \
          --vault="homelab" \
          "password=$PASSPHRASE" \
          "notes=OpenTofu state encryption passphrase for homelab IaC"
        echo "✅ Created 1Password item 'opentofu'"
        echo "The passphrase will be automatically retrieved when running tofu commands"

  tofu:encryption:test:
    desc: "Test state encryption passphrase retrieval"
    cmds:
      - |
        if [ -n "$TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase" ]; then
          echo "✅ State encryption passphrase is set (${#TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase} chars)"
        else
          echo "❌ State encryption passphrase not set"
          echo "Run 'task tofu:encryption:setup' or set TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase"
          exit 1
        fi

  tofu:ssh:
    desc: "SSH to a deployed LXC by app name"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/tofu/ssh.sh {{.APP}}
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:logs:
    desc: "View Docker logs from a deployed app"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/tofu/logs.sh {{.APP}} {{.SERVICE}}
    requires:
      vars: [APP, SERVICE]

  tofu:info:
    desc: "Show OpenTofu IaC status"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/tofu/info.sh

# OpenTofu IaC Commands
# https://taskfile.dev
#
# Each app has its own state file in tofu/apps/<app>/
# Use APP=dashboards|openwebui|portainer|etc to specify which app

version: '3'

vars:
  TOFU_DIR: "tofu"

tasks:
  tofu:init:
    desc: "Initialize OpenTofu for an app (APP=dashboards|openwebui|portainer)"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu init
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:plan:
    desc: "Plan infrastructure changes for an app"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - pwd
      - tofu plan -out=tfplan
    requires:
      vars: [APP]
    preconditions:
      - sh: test -d .terraform
        msg: "Run 'task tofu:init APP={{.APP}}' first"

  tofu:apply:
    desc: "Apply planned infrastructure changes for an app"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu apply tfplan
    requires:
      vars: [APP]
    preconditions:
      - sh: test -f tfplan
        msg: "Run 'task tofu:plan APP={{.APP}}' first"

  tofu:apply:auto:
    desc: "Plan and apply without confirmation"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu apply -auto-approve
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:destroy:
    desc: "Destroy an app's infrastructure"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - echo "⚠️  This will destroy {{.APP}} infrastructure!"
      - tofu destroy
    requires:
      vars: [APP]
    prompt: "Are you sure you want to destroy {{.APP}}?"

  tofu:output:
    desc: "Show infrastructure outputs for an app"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu output
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:state:
    desc: "List all resources in an app's state"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu state list
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:import:
    desc: "Import existing resource into state (APP, ADDR, ID)"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu import '{{.ADDR}}' '{{.ID}}'
    requires:
      vars: [APP, ADDR, ID]

  tofu:fmt:
    desc: "Format all Terraform files"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu fmt -recursive

  tofu:validate:
    desc: "Validate an app's configuration"
    dir: "{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/{{.APP}}"
    cmds:
      - tofu validate
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:encryption:setup:
    desc: "Set up state encryption passphrase in 1Password"
    cmds:
      - |
        echo "Creating 1Password item for state encryption..."
        PASSPHRASE=$(openssl rand -base64 32)
        op item create \
          --category=password \
          --title="opentofu" \
          --vault="homelab" \
          "password=$PASSPHRASE" \
          "notes=OpenTofu state encryption passphrase for homelab IaC"
        echo "✅ Created 1Password item 'opentofu'"
        echo "The passphrase will be automatically retrieved when running tofu commands"

  tofu:encryption:test:
    desc: "Test state encryption passphrase retrieval"
    cmds:
      - |
        if [ -n "$TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase" ]; then
          echo "✅ State encryption passphrase is set (${#TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase} chars)"
        else
          echo "❌ State encryption passphrase not set"
          echo "Run 'task tofu:encryption:setup' or set TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase"
          exit 1
        fi

  tofu:ssh:
    desc: "SSH to a deployed LXC by app name"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/tofu/ssh.sh {{.APP}}
    requires:
      vars: [APP]

  tofu:logs:
    desc: "View Docker logs from a deployed app"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/tofu/logs.sh {{.APP}} {{.SERVICE}}
    requires:
      vars: [APP, SERVICE]

  tofu:info:
    desc: "Show OpenTofu IaC status"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/tofu/info.sh

## Proxmox Backup Server LXC Container Installation

### Installation Methods

**Basic Installation in LXC Container:**
One approach is to apply the ID mappings before installing PBS. Create a standard Debian 12 container, then install PBS.(no content)The general process involves downloading a Debian template and installing a minimal container (2 GB RAM, 8 GB HD), then choosing the container/Options/Features and enabling NFS.

**Installation Steps:**
The installation process includes:
- Run `apt-get update` and `apt-get dist-upgrade`
- Install the repo key
- Add the PBS debian package repo to /etc/apt/sources.list
- Install the PBS-server software with `apt-get install proxmox-backup-server`(no content)After installation, put the NFS-share into /etc/fstab to automatically mount it at reboot.

### Important Considerations

You can run PBS in a container. It's not recommended mostly from an infrastructure point of view - if this server goes down you now don't have access to your backups. Other than that it works perfectly.(no content)LXC containers are lighter weight than VMs. They're not as customizable as a full VM but work well for PBS.

### Troubleshooting

If PBS didn't start up, check that proxmox-backup-proxy is running - that's the program that gives you the web-based GUI. It's part of the proxmox-backup-server Debian package and should have been started by systemd using the service file at /lib/systemd/system/proxmox-backup-proxy.service.(no content)Running `journalctl -xeu proxmox-backup-proxy.service` may provide helpful messages if there are issues.

### NFS Storage Configuration

You need to enable NFS in the options of the container. Log in as root@pam and then choose the container/Options/Features and then enable NFS.(no content)For NFS server settings (including TrueNAS), the main settings needed are: root/wheel permissions on the dataset and no_root_squash in the NFS share settings.

### 2025 Updates

As of 2025, the Proxmox VE Helper-Scripts repo (RIP tteck) only has PBS LXC support. Installing PBS as a VM takes a little more work as there's no automated script available.(no content)In late 2025, Docker VMs still provide the most flexibility and support for real-world container stacks. LXC containers still have a place and provide great performance and low overhead but are not compatible without conversion with OCI container images.

### Alternative: Installing on PVE Host

If you want to use VMs or LXC, it is a better idea to install Proxmox PVE and then PBS along PVE. This approach is recommended for very small deployments with just one server.(no content)You can add the PBS repo, then run `apt install proxmox-backup-server` directly on a PVE host.

Here are the search results for installing Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) on the same node as Proxmox VE (PVE):

## Installing PBS on a PVE Host (Same Node)

### Can It Be Done?
Yes, you can just install the package from the repositories.(no content)The network settings will be the same as your PVE host, and port 8007 will start hosting the web GUI for backup server.(no content)PVE listens on port 8006 and PBS utilizes port 8007, so there's no conflict.

### Installation Steps

**On an existing PVE host**, you can install PBS as a plugin:

1. Add the PBS repository to your sources.list by adding lines like:
   ```
   # PBS pbs-no-subscription repository provided by proxmox.com
   deb http://download.proxmox.com/debian/pbs bookworm pbs-no-subscription
   ```

2. Then execute the following commands to update the package list and install:
   ```
   apt update
   apt install proxmox-backup-server
   ```
   Now you can call up and configure the installed PBS with the IP address of the server and port 8007 in a browser.

### Configuring PVE to Use the Local PBS

You need to define a new storage with type 'pbs' on your Proxmox VE node. For example:
```
pvesm add pbs store2 --server localhost --datastore store2
pvesm set store2 --username user1@pbs --password <secret>
```(no content)To integrate via the GUI: log in to your Proxmox VE GUI with the Datacenter node selected, click the Storage option, click the Add button, and choose Proxmox Backup Server. Note that just entering the username is not sufficient; you also need to specify the realm (e.g., root@pam).

### Important Considerations

It is generally not a good idea to store backups on the same physical system as live-data.(no content)Be careful though, when your node fails you don't have access to your machines AND their backups!(no content)For shared resources, if you have enough to spare you shouldn't have any bottleneck. System requirements for backup server are not so much - you should ideally make sure you have good disks.

### Namespace Recommendation for Multi-Host Setups

If your PBS instance will be backing up more than one PVE host, you should isolate them by namespace because PBS groups its backups by CT/VM ID, regardless of which host it came from. For example, ct/101 on host 1 might be different from ct/101 on host 2. Using namespaces (e.g., host1, host2) keeps the backups uniquely named and preserved separately.

### PBS Features

All backups within PBS are deduplicated and incremental by design. No need to enable anything.(no content)The Proxmox Backup Server integration provides advanced features, including the ability to combine full backups and data deduplication, perform client-side encryption, back up to tape or S3 object storage, and sync with other offsite Proxmox Backup Server installations.

content.text:
Based on my research, there are two approaches for PBS:

1. **Install PBS directly on the PVE host** (simpler, recommended for single-node homelabs)
2. **Install PBS in an LXC container** (more isolated, but adds complexity)

For your homelab, installing PBS directly on the Proxmox host is the simplest approach since:
- It avoids the "backups fail when backup server fails" problem (PBS runs on the hypervisor)
- No additional container to manage
- Storage is already available on the host
- Web UI on port 8007 (PVE is on 8006)

Let me create a script-based approach to install PBS on your Proxmox host, rather than managing it via OpenTofu (since PBS isn't a container):

input.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Install Proxmox Backup Server on PVE Host
# =============================================================================
# This script installs PBS alongside PVE on the same host.
# PBS will run on port 8007 (PVE uses 8006).
#
# Usage: ssh root@homelab 'bash -s' < scripts/pbs/install.sh
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail

echo "=== Installing Proxmox Backup Server ==="

# Check if running on Proxmox
if ! command -v pveversion &> /dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: This script must be run on a Proxmox VE host"
    exit 1
fi

# Check if PBS is already installed
if command -v proxmox-backup-manager &> /dev/null; then
    echo "PBS is already installed:"
    proxmox-backup-manager version
    exit 0
fi

echo "1. Adding PBS repository..."
# Add PBS no-subscription repository
cat > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/pbs-no-subscription.list << 'EOF'
# PBS pbs-no-subscription repository provided by proxmox.com
deb http://download.proxmox.com/debian/pbs bookworm pbs-no-subscription
EOF

echo "2. Updating package lists..."
apt-get update

echo "3. Installing Proxmox Backup Server..."
apt-get install -y proxmox-backup-server

echo "4. Verifying installation..."
proxmox-backup-manager version

echo ""
echo "=== PBS Installation Complete ==="
echo ""
echo "Web UI: https://$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'):8007"
echo "Login: root@pam (same password as PVE)"
echo ""
echo "Next steps:"
echo "1. Access the PBS web UI"
echo "2. Create a datastore (e.g., on /tank/backups/pbs)"
echo "3. Configure PVE to use PBS storage"
echo ""

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Create PBS Datastore
# =============================================================================
# Creates a datastore on the existing ZFS pool for PBS backups.
#
# Usage: ssh root@homelab 'bash -s' < scripts/pbs/create-datastore.sh
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail

DATASTORE_NAME="${1:-homelab}"
DATASTORE_PATH="${2:-/tank/backups/pbs}"

echo "=== Creating PBS Datastore ==="
echo "Name: $DATASTORE_NAME"
echo "Path: $DATASTORE_PATH"

# Check if PBS is installed
if ! command -v proxmox-backup-manager &> /dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: PBS is not installed. Run install.sh first."
    exit 1
fi

# Create datastore directory
echo "1. Creating datastore directory..."
mkdir -p "$DATASTORE_PATH"

# Check if datastore already exists
if proxmox-backup-manager datastore list | grep -q "^${DATASTORE_NAME}"; then
    echo "Datastore '$DATASTORE_NAME' already exists:"
    proxmox-backup-manager datastore show "$DATASTORE_NAME"
    exit 0
fi

echo "2. Creating PBS datastore..."
proxmox-backup-manager datastore create "$DATASTORE_NAME" "$DATASTORE_PATH"

echo "3. Configuring garbage collection schedule (daily at 5 AM)..."
proxmox-backup-manager datastore update "$DATASTORE_NAME" --gc-schedule "daily 05:00"

echo "4. Configuring prune schedule (weekly on Sunday at 6 AM)..."
proxmox-backup-manager datastore update "$DATASTORE_NAME" --prune-schedule "weekly sun 06:00"

# Set retention policy: 7 daily, 4 weekly, 3 monthly
echo "5. Setting retention policy..."
proxmox-backup-manager datastore update "$DATASTORE_NAME" \
    --keep-daily 7 \
    --keep-weekly 4 \
    --keep-monthly 3

echo ""
echo "=== Datastore Created ==="
proxmox-backup-manager datastore show "$DATASTORE_NAME"
echo ""
echo "Next: Add PBS storage to PVE using:"
echo "  pvesm add pbs pbs-$DATASTORE_NAME --server localhost --datastore $DATASTORE_NAME --username root@pam"
echo ""

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Add PBS Storage to PVE
# =============================================================================
# Configures PVE to use the local PBS instance for backups.
#
# Usage: ssh root@homelab 'bash -s' < scripts/pbs/add-pve-storage.sh
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail

DATASTORE_NAME="${1:-homelab}"
STORAGE_NAME="${2:-pbs-homelab}"

echo "=== Adding PBS Storage to PVE ==="
echo "PBS Datastore: $DATASTORE_NAME"
echo "PVE Storage Name: $STORAGE_NAME"

# Check if storage already exists
if pvesm status | grep -q "^${STORAGE_NAME}"; then
    echo "Storage '$STORAGE_NAME' already exists:"
    pvesm status | grep "^${STORAGE_NAME}"
    exit 0
fi

# Prompt for password
echo ""
echo "Enter the PBS password for root@pam:"
read -s PBS_PASSWORD
echo ""

echo "1. Adding PBS storage to PVE..."
pvesm add pbs "$STORAGE_NAME" \
    --server localhost \
    --datastore "$DATASTORE_NAME" \
    --username root@pam \
    --password "$PBS_PASSWORD" \
    --content backup \
    --fingerprint "$(proxmox-backup-manager cert info 2>/dev/null | grep Fingerprint | awk '{print $2}')"

echo "2. Verifying storage..."
pvesm status | grep "^${STORAGE_NAME}"

echo ""
echo "=== PBS Storage Added ==="
echo ""
echo "You can now:"
echo "1. Go to Datacenter > Backup in PVE web UI"
echo "2. Create backup jobs using '$STORAGE_NAME' storage"
echo "3. Or migrate existing vzdump jobs to use PBS"
echo ""

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# Install Proxmox Backup Server on PVE Host
# =============================================================================
# This script installs PBS alongside PVE on the same host.
# PBS will run on port 8007 (PVE uses 8006).
#
# Usage: ssh root@homelab 'bash -s' < scripts/pbs/install.sh
# =============================================================================

set -euo pipefail

echo "=== Installing Proxmox Backup Server ==="

# Check if running on Proxmox
if ! command -v pveversion &> /dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: This script must be run on a Proxmox VE host"
    exit 1
fi

# Check if PBS is already installed
if command -v proxmox-backup-manager &> /dev/null; then
    echo "PBS is already installed:"
    proxmox-backup-manager version
    exit 0
fi

echo "1. Adding PBS repository..."
# Add PBS no-subscription repository
cat > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/pbs-no-subscription.list << 'EOF'
# PBS pbs-no-subscription repository provided by proxmox.com
deb http://download.proxmox.com/debian/pbs bookworm pbs-no-subscription
EOF

echo "2. Updating package lists..."
apt-get update

echo "3. Installing Proxmox Backup Server..."
apt-get install -y proxmox-backup-server

echo "4. Verifying installation..."
proxmox-backup-manager version

echo ""
echo "=== PBS Installation Complete ==="
echo ""
echo "Web UI: https://$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'):8007"
echo "Login: root@pam (same password as PVE)"
echo ""
echo "Next steps:"
echo "1. Access the PBS web UI"
echo "2. Create a datastore (e.g., on /tank/backups/pbs)"
echo "3. Configure PVE to use PBS storage"
echo ""

# Homelab Infrastructure Automation
# https://taskfile.dev

version: '3'

vars:
  PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.TASKFILE_DIR}}"
  TOFU_DIR: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}/tofu"

env:
  # State encryption passphrase - MUST be TF_VAR because encryption runs before providers
  # All other secrets are now fetched via 1Password provider directly in OpenTofu
  TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase:
    sh: |
      if [ -n "$TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase" ]; then
        echo "$TF_VAR_state_encryption_passphrase"
      else
        op read "op://homelab/opentofu/password" 2>/dev/null || echo ""
      fi

# =============================================================================
# Included Taskfiles (flattened into main namespace)
# =============================================================================
includes:
  tofu:
    taskfile: ./tasks/tofu.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"
  backup:
    taskfile: ./tasks/backup.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"
  cloud:
    taskfile: ./tasks/cloud.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"
  template:
    taskfile: ./tasks/template.yml
    flatten: true
    vars:
      PROJECT_ROOT: "{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}"

tasks:
  # ===========================================================================
  # Desktop LXC (Temporary GUI for Downloads)
  # ===========================================================================

  desktop:create:
    desc: "Create temporary GUI desktop LXC for downloading Google Takeout"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/desktop-lxc/create.sh

  desktop:destroy:
    desc: "Destroy temporary GUI desktop LXC"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/desktop-lxc/destroy.sh

  desktop:info:
    desc: "Show VNC connection info for desktop LXC"
    cmds:
      - |
        IP=$(ssh root@homelab "pct exec 600 -- ip -4 addr show eth0 | grep inet | awk '{print \$2}' | cut -d/ -f1" 2>/dev/null)
        if [ -z "$IP" ]; then
          echo "Desktop LXC (600) is not running or does not exist."
          echo "Run 'task desktop:create' first."
          exit 1
        fi
        echo "=== Desktop LXC VNC Connection ==="
        echo ""
        echo "VNC Host: $IP:5901"
        echo ""
        echo "macOS: Open Finder, Cmd+K, enter vnc://$IP:5901"
        echo ""
        echo "Downloads save to: /downloads (mounted to /tank/photo-import)"

  desktop:restart-vnc:
    desc: "Restart VNC server on desktop LXC"
    cmds:
      - |
        echo "Restarting VNC server..."
        ssh root@homelab "pct exec 600 -- bash -c 'vncserver -kill :1 2>/dev/null || true; vncserver :1 -geometry 1920x1080 -depth 24 -localhost no'"
        echo "VNC server restarted on display :1"

  # ===========================================================================
  # Authelia Operations
  # ===========================================================================

  authelia:secrets:
    desc: "Generate Authelia secrets from 1Password"
    cmds:
      - |
        SECRETS_DIR="{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}/tofu/apps/authelia/deploy/secrets"
        mkdir -p "$SECRETS_DIR"
        echo "Fetching secrets from 1Password..."
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/jwt_secret" > "$SECRETS_DIR/jwt_secret"
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/session_secret" > "$SECRETS_DIR/session_secret"
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/storage_encryption_key" > "$SECRETS_DIR/storage_encryption_key"
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/oidc_hmac_secret" > "$SECRETS_DIR/oidc_hmac_secret"
        op read "op://homelab/authelia/oidc_private_key" > "$SECRETS_DIR/oidc_private_key"
        chmod 600 "$SECRETS_DIR"/*
        echo "Secrets written to $SECRETS_DIR"

  authelia:users:
    desc: "Generate Authelia users database from 1Password"
    cmds:
      - |
        USERS_FILE="{{.PROJECT_ROOT}}/tofu/apps/authelia/deploy/authelia/users_database.yml"
        HASH=$(op read "op://homelab/authelia/admin_password_hash")
        if [ "$HASH" = "PLACEHOLDER_RUN_DOCKER_TO_GENERATE" ]; then
          echo "ERROR: admin_password_hash is still a placeholder."
          echo "Run: docker run --rm -it authelia/authelia:latest authelia crypto hash generate argon2"
          echo "Then update 1Password: op item edit authelia --vault=homelab 'admin_password_hash=YOUR_HASH'"
          exit 1
        fi
        echo "users:" > "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "  admin:" >> "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "    displayname: \"Admin\"" >> "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "    email: admin@homelab.rambtech.dev" >> "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "    password: \"$HASH\"" >> "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "    groups:" >> "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "      - admins" >> "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "      - users" >> "$USERS_FILE"
        echo "Users database written to $USERS_FILE"

  authelia:setup:
    desc: "Full Authelia setup (secrets + users)"
    cmds:
      - task: authelia:secrets
      - task: authelia:users
      - echo "Authelia setup complete. Run 'task tofu:apply APP=authelia' to deploy."

  # ===========================================================================
  # AdGuard DNS Operations
  # ===========================================================================

  adguard:test:
    desc: "Test DNS resolution for homelab domains"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/sync/adguard-sync.sh test

  # ===========================================================================
  # Immich Importer Setup
  # ===========================================================================

  immich-importer:secrets:
    desc: "Generate immich-importer terraform.tfvars from 1Password"
    cmds:
      - |
        TFVARS="{{.TOFU_DIR}}/apps/immich-importer/terraform.tfvars"
        echo "Fetching secrets from 1Password..."

        B2_KEY_ID=$(op read "op://homelab/Backblaze/keyId")
        B2_APP_KEY=$(op read "op://homelab/Backblaze/b2_app_key")
        CRYPT_PASS=$(op read "op://homelab/backblaze-rclone-crypt/password_obscured")
        CRYPT_SALT=$(op read "op://homelab/backblaze-rclone-crypt/password2_obscured")
        IMMICH_KEY=$(op read "op://homelab/ecdglhzani6r76zniumdzrjdoy/immich-go")

        cat > "$TFVARS" << EOF
        # Auto-generated from 1Password - DO NOT COMMIT
        b2_account_id          = "$B2_KEY_ID"
        b2_application_key     = "$B2_APP_KEY"
        rclone_crypt_password  = "$CRYPT_PASS"
        rclone_crypt_password2 = "$CRYPT_SALT"
        immich_api_key         = "$IMMICH_KEY"
        cloud_backup_schedule  = "0 3 * * 0,3"
        EOF

        echo "terraform.tfvars written to $TFVARS"

  immich-importer:cron:status:
    desc: "Show cron job status on immich-importer LXC"
    cmds:
      - ssh root@homelab "pct exec 303 -- crontab -l"

  # ===========================================================================
  # IP Address Management
  # ===========================================================================

  ip:next:
    desc: "Show the next available IP address for new LXC deployment"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/ip/next.sh

  ip:list:
    desc: "Show all allocated IP addresses"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/ip/list.sh

  # ===========================================================================
  # Cleanup & Maintenance
  # ===========================================================================

  cleanup:
    desc: "Clean up temporary files, backups, and cruft (dry run)"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/cleanup.sh

  cleanup:run:
    desc: "Clean up temporary files, backups, and cruft (actually delete)"
    cmds:
      - ./scripts/cleanup.sh --run

     2→# Create temporary GUI desktop LXC for Google Takeout downloads
     3→# Downloads directly to NAS storage via VNC desktop with Chrome
     4→
     5→set -e
     6→
     7→CONTAINER_ID=600
     8→CONTAINER_NAME="desktop-tmp"

    10→PROXMOX_HOST="root@homelab"

    12→echo "=== Creating Temporary Desktop LXC ==="

    14→

    17→    echo "Container $CONTAINER_ID already exists."
    18→    echo "Run 'task desktop:destroy' first, or use 'task desktop:info' to get connection details."
    19→    exit 1
    20→fi
    21→
    22→echo "[1/6] Creating LXC container (privileged for NAS mount)..."
    23→ssh "$PROXMOX_HOST" "pct create $CONTAINER_ID $TEMPLATE \
    24→    --hostname $CONTAINER_NAME \
    25→    --cores 4 \
    26→    --memory 4096 \
    27→    --swap 512 \
    28→    --rootfs nvme-containers:32 \
    29→    --net0 name=eth0,bridge=vmbr0,ip=dhcp,type=veth \
    30→    --features nesting=1,keyctl=1 \
    31→    --unprivileged 0 \
    32→    --onboot 0"
    33→
    34→echo "[2/6] Adding NAS mount point..."
    35→ssh "$PROXMOX_HOST" "pct set $CONTAINER_ID -mp0 /tank/photo-import,mp=/downloads"
    36→
    37→echo "[3/6] Starting container..."
    38→ssh "$PROXMOX_HOST" "pct start $CONTAINER_ID"
    39→
    40→# Wait for container to get IP
    41→echo "    Waiting for network..."
    42→sleep 10
    43→
    44→# Fix DNS (Tailscale DNS may not resolve external hosts)
    45→ssh "$PROXMOX_HOST" "pct exec $CONTAINER_ID -- bash -c 'echo nameserver 8.8.8.8 > /etc/resolv.conf'"
    46→
    47→# Get container IP
    48→CONTAINER_IP=$(ssh "$PROXMOX_HOST" "pct exec $CONTAINER_ID -- ip -4 addr show eth0 | grep inet | awk '{print \$2}' | cut -d/ -f1")
    49→if [ -z "$CONTAINER_IP" ]; then
    50→    echo "ERROR: Could not get container IP. Container may still be starting."
    51→    echo "Try: ssh $PROXMOX_HOST 'pct exec $CONTAINER_ID -- ip addr'"
    52→    exit 1

    54→echo "    Container IP: $CONTAINER_IP"
    55→
    56→echo "[4/6] Installing XFCE desktop + VNC..."
    57→ssh "$PROXMOX_HOST" "pct exec $CONTAINER_ID -- bash -c '
    58→    export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
    59→    apt-get update
    60→    apt-get upgrade -y
    61→    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    62→        xfce4 \
    63→        xfce4-terminal \

    65→        tigervnc-standalone-server \
    66→        tigervnc-common \
    67→        tigervnc-tools \

    69→        gnupg \
    70→        ca-certificates
    71→'"
    72→
    73→echo "[5/6] Installing Google Chrome..."
    74→ssh "$PROXMOX_HOST" "pct exec $CONTAINER_ID -- bash -c '
    75→    wget -q -O - https://dl-ssl.google.com/linux/linux_signing_key.pub | gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/google-chrome.gpg
    76→    echo \"deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/google-chrome.gpg] http://dl.google.com/linux/chrome/deb/ stable main\" > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/google-chrome.list
